failure_modes: Post-NDE aftereffect passages: 'now the birds sing more vividly to me', playing with butterflies/cats back on earth (4 passages)

Metaphor and commentary: Plato using 'birds flying' as an analogy for out-of-body travel; Eben-Alexander-style philosophy about 'the trees, the birds, the sky' as an internal construct
Passages with no animal at all that matched on garden/paradise vocabulary (flowers filling a room; a waterfall of stars; 'lint particles')

best_quote.text: There were no people there. There were only animals, birds singing, little animals chirping, and squirrels and chipmunks and rabbits.

failure_modes: Dominant junk: ordinary biography 'walking down the path to my car' / 'walking down the road' before the accident — 8 of 24 passages, including three near-duplicate retellings of the same car-crash prologue
Metaphorical paths: 'that path led me to plant medicine', 'the path is unwinding', 'mankind is on a path of destruction'
Real-world trails: a mountaineering route, a jungle clinic path, a watchmaker errand
Secondhand: an angel-escorted 'pathway through the meadows of heaven' narrated about a third party (Jim), and a hospice nurse's story of a dying boy seen walking a path

best_quote.text: as I'm walking down the paths, and I'm walking towards this city, by the size of the buildings being this big over in the distance

failure_modes: Ordinary social belonging: not fitting in at school/neighbourhood, 'I don't belong here' said at an IANDS meeting
Interviewer-supplied wording: two passages where 'sense of belonging' appears only in the question and the answer describes joy/well-being instead
Book-plug and facilitator commentary about shared-death work giving people 'a sense of belonging'
Opposite sense of the same phrase: 'I don't belong here' spoken IN heaven out of unworthiness (he's made a terrible mistake), which is the inverse of earth-exile
Belonging in hell ('this is where I belonged, this is what I deserved') — same word, different place

best_quote.text: It was, it was being home. This is where I fit. This is where I belong. This is where I was totally loved.

failure_modes: Recurring junk: the experiencer's OWN restored/young spirit body ('I looked 25 at 40', 'my hands looked like I was 18', looking younger in the mirror afterwards) — 4 passages. That is a real feature but a different one; it should not be counted as 'how the dead appear'
Descriptions of Jesus's appearance (healthy, in his prime, not battered) and of an unidentified old-bearded being with young skin — beings, not deceased loved ones
Pure biography (a dinner shift with stomach pain) and post-NDE self-talk about 'the Alyssa that was no longer sick'
Channel commentary generalising that 'loved ones look like they're in the prime of their life' rather than a firsthand sighting
One passage framed explicitly as a dream in a hospital room

best_quote.text: My father was also standing. I had never in my life seen him stand or walk. He looked vibrant and in the prime of his life, and I was ecstatic. He was healed.

failure_modes: Garden as metaphor: 'the Earth is a giant garden and we all live in it'; a prayer asking God to 'turn my soul into a garden'; a grief poem's 'you're in the kitchen, you're in the garden'
Ordinary gardening/meditation advice ('sit with a cup of coffee looking out into your garden')
Generalisation about what other people see ('some people see beautiful gardens with flowers, others go to the beach')

best_quote.text: If you can picture the most perfect English garden, perfectly manicured, perfect grass, trees, flowers, I mean, absolutely gorgeous.

audits.note: This id appears twice in the manifest slice (matched 206 and matched 166) but only one packet file exists at audit/the-garden.txt; audited once.

failure_modes: '360' in ordinary use: giant photographs placed 360 around a courtroom
'360-degree viewpoint' as a metaphor for perspective-taking (walking in another's shoes; being poor and being rich)
Generalised teaching that 'when we are out of our bodies we have that 360 degree perspective' — meaning complete understanding, not literal vision
Light 'spreading out in all directions' — a description of the light's extent, not of an omnidirectional visual field (2 near-duplicate passages)
A 360-degree vision event that happened while driving a car, days after a funeral — an after-death-communication, not the NDE

best_quote.text: I have 360-degree vision. Like, I can see everything around me, behind me, below me, above me.

failure_modes: Passages that mention 'life review' with no screen, movie or projector at all — the regex appears to match the review itself rather than its staging
Explicit denials of the cinema frame: 'it's often described as a film, but for me it wasn't a film, it was all the information at once'
Generalised teaching about what everyone does after death ('you go with your team of guides and you watch the movie of your life')
Pop-culture jokes ('like that movie Defending Your Life', 'a Netflix documentary about your life')
'Movies/films' as ordinary-life content inside the review — school Duck-and-Cover films, 'teachers, schools, movies, media'
A film reel of the whole earth's history that the experiencer explicitly says was NOT a life review

best_quote.text: I found myself standing in a kind of gray mist, and then I knew. I knew that I had died.

failure_modes: Dominant junk: the idiom 'out into the universe' / 'into outer space' used figuratively — thoughts going out into the universe, 'kick the word should out into outer space', signs that 'go out into the universe', souls who will 'go out into the universe and do good', meditation to 'get out into the universe at large'. Six passages, all of them pure figure of speech
Commentary about NASA spacecraft and planetary frequencies
Trance-journey and dream travel to space that the speaker frames as neither an NDE nor an OBE
Passages where 'space' is only the setting of the life review (bubbles of lifetimes) with no planet, stars or recession described

best_quote.text: My spirit was traveling very fast, and I saw the Earth below me, and I seemed to be amidst the stars.

failure_modes: Dominant junk: plain out-of-body ceiling hovering ('I floated up to the corner of the ceiling and looked down at my body') — 7 passages. That is the leaving-the-body feature, which has its own packet; it is not the ascent past the room into sky and starfield that this claim describes
Secondhand narration of someone else's rise (a host recounting Robert's drowning, a daughter quoting her father, a third-person retelling of a woman floating up a stairway)
A nitrous-oxide float out of a dentist's chair and a meditative OBE — lift, but not during a near-death event
Hovering with no upward motion (suspended 20 feet over a desert scene)
One passage where the lift is immediately followed by entering a cylinder/tunnel, which contradicts the 'without a tunnel' qualifier the claim rests on

best_quote.text: Slowly I floated upward, out of the room and building, above the trees, and up into a black, star-filled sky.

failure_modes: Host intro boilerplate summarising the guest's story in the third person ('he found himself carried towards what he thought was a star brighter than ten thousand suns')

A second-person literary/generalised passage ('The light beckons you... brighter than a million suns, and yet it does not blind or burn you') which reads as a written set piece about what happens rather than a firsthand report

best_quote.text: The light was brighter than hundreds of suns, but it did not hurt my eyes.

failure_modes: Ordinary reincarnation talk with no NDE content: children who remember being murdered in a past life, a six-year-old who can fly a plane, a mother's account of her son's memories
Post-NDE healing practice: 'I help them clear past lives', reading whether a client's illness comes from a past life
Past-life memories that arrived AFTER the experience ('I've seen a few of my past lives since this experience', 'I sat on my couch and I saw it')
Researcher and interviewer commentary about how often a 'past life review' occurs in NDE typologies
Explicit denials: 'I didn't have a real past life review', 'some people say they have past life reviews — for me it was more like a glass of water'
'My past life' used to mean simply this life up to now ('visions of my life, my past life... scenes of my life going before me')
Seeing ANOTHER person's past lives (a bus driver's) rather than one's own review — 2 passages
One textbook-perfect match for the claim (an arena with sections showing several simultaneous lifetimes) that is a retelling of Andy Petro's NDE by someone else
